name: Cleft lip and palate
fullName: Cleft lip and palate with congenital anomalies
subtitle: Paediatric surgical conditions

chapters.title: Basics

chapters.blurb: Born with it, and the pregnancy behind it

skill.particulars.demographics.expect: Expect an infant or young child brought by the mother, with the defect present since birth. Consanguinity, absent antenatal folate, and tobacco or alcohol exposure in early pregnancy all raise the prior, and a family history of clefts or lip pits points to a familial form.

chapters.title: Patient particulars

chapters.blurb: The visible gap, and the hidden functions behind it

skill.hx.chief_complaints.expect: Expect the mother's words to centre on the visible gap and on feeding: a long feed with milk escaping through the nose, coughing or tiring, and faltering weight. Noisy breathing, ear discharge and poor response to sound are the associated complaints that decide urgency.

chapters.title: History of presenting illness

chapters.blurb: The pregnancy that made the cleft
chapters.title: Past, personal, drug and family history

chapters.blurb: Growth first, then the search for anything beyond the cleft

skill.gen.appearance.expect: Look for an infant who may be small for age, with any feature beyond the cleft itself: low set ears, limb differences, or unusual facies. Faltering growth is the general sign that feeding support cannot wait.

skill.gen.vitals.expect: Expect vitals appropriate for age, with the weight and its trend mattering more than any single reading. Fast breathing, chest recession or pauses in breathing point to airway obstruction, especially where the jaw is small, and outrank every local finding.

chapters.title: General examination

chapters.blurb: Lip, alveolus, palate and nodes, in that order

skill.exam.surg.maxilla.expect: Expect a notched or gapped alveolus on the cleft side, and in bilateral complete clefts a forward placed premaxilla. Feel the alveolar segments and note their displacement, since this decides the orthodontic plan.

skill.exam.surg.buccal_mucosa.expect: Expect the lip gap to run into the nostril floor in a complete cleft, with a flattened nostril wing and a pulled columella on that side. Note whether the cleft runs the full height to the nostril or stops short, and whether the septum hangs free or is attached to one side.

skill.exam.surg.floor_of_mouth.expect: Expect the palate cleft to declare its full extent with the mouth open and the tongue depressed: uvula alone, soft palate, or hard and soft palate together. Where the mucosa looks intact, look for the submucous triad of a split uvula, midline translucency and a notched hard palate.

skill.exam.surg.cervical_nodes.expect: Expect no nodes in an uncomplicated cleft. Enlarged submental or submandibular nodes mean current mouth infection or another pathology, and both sides are examined because lymph drainage crosses the midline.

skill.reasoning.cleft.basics.title: What an orofacial cleft is
skill.reasoning.cleft.basics.oneLine: A fusion failure of early pregnancy, in the lip, the palate, or both
skill.reasoning.cleft.basics.why: Lip and palate look like one disease because they often occur together, but they fuse at different times and from different parts of the face. Knowing which process failed tells you what to look for next: a lip cleft points to the nose and alveolus, a palate cleft to feeding, hearing and speech.

teach.heading: A failure of fusion, in the first weeks
teach.body:
The lip forms when the medial nasal process meets the maxillary process on each side. If they fail to unite, a cleft lip results, running from the red margin upward, and it may stop short of the nostril or run the full height into it.

The palate forms when the two palatine shelves rise, meet in the midline and fuse with the premaxilla from the frontonasal process. Failure here gives a cleft palate, from a split uvula at the mild end to a wide gap through soft and hard palate at the severe end.

teach.heading: Lip only, palate only, or both
teach.body:
A cleft may involve the lip alone, the palate alone, or both together, and each may sit on one side or on both. A bilateral complete lip cleft often pushes the premaxilla forward between the two gaps, which is expected and not a separate tumour.

Cleft lip with or without cleft palate, and isolated cleft palate, behave as distinct entities with different embryology and different links to syndromes. Saying which one you are dealing with is the first step of every diagnosis.

teach.heading: Isolated or part of a syndrome
teach.body:
Most clefts are isolated, but some belong to recognised syndromes, so every child needs a check for other anomalies of the heart, limbs, ears and growth. Lower lip pits point to Van der Woude syndrome, the commonest familial form.

A small receding jaw with the tongue falling back and a palate cleft makes Pierre Robin sequence, where the airway matters more than the gap. Missing the syndrome while admiring the cleft is the classic error.

probes.q: Which two facial processes fail to unite in a cleft lip, and what fails to fuse in a cleft palate?
probes.a: The medial nasal process with the maxillary process in cleft lip, and the two palatine shelves with each other and the premaxilla in cleft palate.

probes.q: Why are cleft lip with palate and isolated cleft palate treated as distinct entities?
probes.a: They arise from different embryological processes at different times, and carry different epidemiology and syndromic associations, so the expected associated problems differ.

probes.q: A newborn has a small jaw, a tongue that falls back, and a cleft palate with noisy breathing. What sequence is this, and what takes priority?
probes.a: Pierre Robin sequence. The airway takes priority over the cleft itself, with positioning and urgent referral before any feeding or repair plan.

sources.source: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.reasoning.cleft.signs.title: The cleft picture at the bedside
skill.reasoning.cleft.signs.oneLine: One gap explains the lip, the nose, the feeding and the speech
skill.reasoning.cleft.signs.why: Students describe the photograph but miss the patient: they grade the lip and forget the palate, the ears and the growth card. Every local sign follows from where fusion failed, and every distant sign follows from what the gap breaks, suction, the seal of the ear tube, or the airway.

teach.heading: Read the lip and the nose together
teach.body:
Judge completeness first. An incomplete cleft stops short of the nostril, while a complete one runs the full height into the nostril floor. Bilateral clefts may carry a forward placed premaxilla between them.

Then read the nose on the cleft side: a flattened wing and a pulled columella. Note whether the septum hangs free in the gap or is attached to one side, since the book method records this in every palate description and the surgeon needs it.

teach.heading: Read the palate in full, including the hidden one
teach.body:
With good light and a spatula, map the extent: uvula alone, soft palate, or soft plus hard palate. Palpate the hard palate for a notch even where the mucosa looks whole.

Where the surface looks intact but feeding or speech suggests a gap, look for the submucous triad: a split uvula, a translucent midline zone, and a palpable notch in the hard palate. This occult cleft is the commonest missed diagnosis in the whole topic.

teach.heading: Read the child, not just the gap
teach.body:
Check growth against the card, because a palatal cleft breaks suction and starves by slow degrees. Watch breathing for noise and recession, and test response to sound, since middle ear fluid follows the cleft through the open ear tube.

Scan for anything beyond the cleft: heart murmur, limb differences, ear shape, and growth pattern. One extra anomaly turns an isolated cleft into a possible syndrome and changes referral, counselling and timing.

probes.q: What three findings make the submucous triad of an occult palate cleft?
probes.a: A bifid or split uvula, a translucent midline zone in the soft palate, and a palpable notch in the posterior hard palate.

probes.q: An incomplete lip cleft and a complete one look similar in a photograph. How do you separate them at the bedside?
probes.a: Trace the gap upward. An incomplete cleft stops short of the nostril, while a complete cleft runs the full height into the nostril floor with flattening of the ala on that side.

probes.q: Explain why a cleft palate causes both feeding difficulty and hearing loss.
probes.a: The gap breaks the oral seal so the infant cannot generate suction for feeding, and it leaves the Eustachian tube open and dysfunctional so fluid collects in the middle ear and conducts sound poorly.

skill.reasoning.cleft.differential.title: Differential diagnosis
skill.reasoning.cleft.differential.oneLine: What else makes a gap, a small jaw, or nasal speech
skill.reasoning.cleft.differential.why: Most gaps are exactly what they look like, but three mimics change management completely: the hidden submucous cleft that explains years of nasal speech, the small jaw whose airway kills before any repair, and the familial syndrome whose lip pits predict the next child.

teach.heading: The hidden cleft and the small jaw
teach.body:
Submucous cleft palate hides under intact mucosa and presents late with feeding trouble, nasal speech or repeated ear disease. A split uvula is the visible clue, confirmed by feeling a notch in the hard palate.

Pierre Robin sequence is a small receding jaw with the tongue falling back plus a palate cleft, presenting with noisy breathing, feeding choking and apnoeic pauses. The jaw, not the palate, is the diagnosis that matters, because the airway comes first.

teach.heading: The familial and the rare gaps
teach.body:
Van der Woude syndrome pairs a cleft with pits of the lower lip and runs strongly in families. Finding pits in the baby or either parent turns counselling for the next pregnancy upside down, so the lips of both parents are part of this examination.

Atypical facial clefts run obliquely from the mouth toward the eye along failed fusion lines, and median clefts split the midline structures. Both are rare, need a craniofacial unit, and must never be confused with an ordinary lip cleft.

teach.heading: Nasal speech and discharge that are not a cleft
teach.body:
Velopharyngeal insufficiency from other causes gives the same nasal speech and nasal fluid escape without any visible gap, after adenoid surgery, in muscle weakness, or after a repaired cleft that still leaks. Nasendoscopy separates a short palate from a poorly moving one.

An isolated split uvula without feeding or speech trouble needs no treatment, only watching. Operating on every bifid uvula would harm children who were never going to suffer from it.

probes.q: Name four conditions in the differential of an orofacial cleft presentation.
probes.a: Submucous cleft palate, Pierre Robin sequence, Van der Woude syndrome, atypical facial cleft, isolated bifid uvula, and velopharyngeal insufficiency from other causes.

probes.q: A seven year old has nasal speech and repeated ear infections with a normal looking palate. What do you look for?
probes.a: A submucous cleft: split uvula, midline translucency and a palpable hard palate notch, with audiology for the middle ear fluid that explains the infections.

rubric.text: Offers a differential spanning hidden, syndromic, atypical and functional causes
Identifies Pierre Robin sequence as the airway-first diagnosis
Uses lip pits and family pattern to recognise Van der Woude syndrome

skill.investigation.cleft.workup.title: Confirming the extent and hunting the associated problems
skill.investigation.cleft.workup.oneLine: The eyes confirm the gap, the ears and genes decide the future
skill.investigation.cleft.workup.why: The cleft itself is a clinical diagnosis that needs no scan to confirm, so every investigation must earn its place by answering a different question: is there a syndrome, can the child hear, and what will speech and teeth need. Ordering a scan of the gap itself wastes the family's money.

teach.heading: What to order, and the question each answers
teach.body:
Prenatal ultrasound can detect a lip cleft and opens counselling before birth, though a palate-only cleft often escapes it. After birth, a full newborn examination for other anomalies outranks every machine test.

Where a syndrome is suspected, genetic evaluation with karyotype or microarray follows. Chromosome detail matters less to the student than knowing when to send: one extra anomaly, growth failure beyond feeding, or a familial pattern.

teach.heading: Ears, speech and teeth have their own workup
teach.body:
Audiology with tympanometry tracks the middle ear fluid that follows almost every palate cleft, and repeats through childhood because the fluid comes and goes while speech is being built. A child who cannot hear cannot learn sounds, whatever the palate repair achieves.

Speech assessment with nasendoscopy or videofluoroscopy maps velopharyngeal closure where nasal speech persists. Dental and orthodontic review with imaging of the alveolus plans bone grafting, timed to the eruption of the permanent canine region teeth.

teach.heading: The workup table
teach.body: Use this table to match each test to its question. If a test answers no question on this list, it does not get ordered.

probes.q: Which investigation confirms the cleft itself?
probes.a: None is needed. The cleft is a clinical diagnosis by inspection and palpation; investigations hunt associated problems, not the gap.

probes.q: When is genetic testing indicated in a child with a cleft?
probes.a: When a syndrome is suspected: an extra anomaly, growth failure beyond feeding difficulty, or a familial pattern such as lip pits.

probes.q: A repaired palate looks closed but speech stays nasal at age five. What investigation next, and why?
probes.a: Speech assessment with nasendoscopy or videofluoroscopy, to map velopharyngeal closure and decide whether secondary surgery such as pharyngoplasty is needed.

sources.source: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.reasoning.cleft.diagnosis.title: Diagnosis and grading: name it fully
skill.reasoning.cleft.diagnosis.oneLine: Defect, side, completeness, Veau group and function in one statement
skill.reasoning.cleft.diagnosis.why: Saying cleft palate stops where the surgeon starts. The repair, its timing and its risks all depend on the full statement: which structures, which side, how complete, and whether feeding, airway and hearing are already suffering.

teach.heading: Five clauses, no shortcuts
teach.body:
A complete diagnosis names the structures involved, the side, and the completeness: complete unilateral left cleft lip and palate, or incomplete right cleft lip with intact palate. Vague words like severe add nothing; the anatomy is the severity.

Append the Veau group for the palate: soft palate only, soft plus hard palate, unilateral complete, or bilateral complete. For example: cleft of soft and hard palate with complete left cleft lip, Veau group three.

teach.heading: Then grade function, not just form
teach.body:
Grade feeding by feed duration, nasal leak and the weight trend. Grade the airway by noise, recession and apnoeic pauses, since obstruction outranks the gap itself. Grade hearing by audiology, not by impression, because fluid fluctuates.

Close with syndrome status: isolated, or syndromic with the named features. A statement that ends without saying isolated or not is unfinished, because follow-up and counselling hinge on it.

probes.q: State a complete diagnosis for a baby with a left lip gap to the nostril and a cleft of soft and hard palate.
probes.a: Complete unilateral left cleft lip and palate, Veau group three, with feeding difficulty and faltering weight, isolated on current assessment.

probes.q: Why does a diagnosis that stops at cleft palate fail the surgeon?
probes.a: Because timing and technique depend on extent, laterality, Veau group, and on feeding, airway and hearing status, none of which the bare label carries.

rubric.text: Names structures, side and completeness without vague terms
States the Veau group for the palate component
Grades feeding, airway and hearing alongside the anatomy

sources.source: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.annex.cleft.classification.title: Classification of clefts: Veau and lip descriptors
skill.annex.cleft.classification.oneLine: The reference table for complete, incomplete, unilateral and bilateral
skill.annex.cleft.classification.why: Cleft notes drown in adjectives unless both sides use the same words. Veau groups the palate, and a fixed set of lip descriptors groups the lip, so a referral letter carries the anatomy instead of an impression.

teach.heading: The lip descriptors
teach.body:
Describe the lip by three facts: side, completeness, and the nose. Unilateral or bilateral, incomplete stopping short of the nostril or complete running into it, with or without nasal flattening and premaxillary forward placement.

Microform clefts show only a notch of the red margin or a scar-like line with nasal asymmetry, and are easily dismissed. Recording the nose in every lip description catches them.

teach.heading: The Veau table
teach.body: Veau classifies the palate from back to front. Groups one and two are midline palate clefts with an intact lip; groups three and four extend through the alveolus with a matching complete lip cleft.

probes.q: What Veau group is a unilateral complete cleft of lip, alveolus and palate?
How does a group two Veau cleft differ from group three?
probes.a: Group two involves soft plus hard palate with an intact lip, while group three is unilateral complete through lip, alveolus and palate.

sources.source: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.treatment.cleft.management.title: Managing the cleft child
skill.treatment.cleft.management.oneLine: Feed today, close in stages, follow hearing, speech and teeth for years
skill.treatment.cleft.management.why: The operation is the visible part of a programme that runs from birth to adolescence. A surgeon who closes the lip but leaves feeding, hearing and speech to chance has treated the photograph while the child falls behind in weight, language and school.

teach.heading: Feeding support comes before any operation
teach.body:
Start feeding help at diagnosis: upright positioning, expressed breast milk by cup and spoon or a soft squeezable bottle, small frequent feeds, and burping pauses. Special teats and feeding plates bridge the gap where suction fails.

Weigh weekly until the curve turns. Poor weight gain delays safe anaesthesia and deepens every later problem, so the growth card is reviewed at every visit, not just weighed and filed.

teach.heading: Surgery is staged around speech and growth
teach.body:
Lip repair comes in early infancy, palate closure later and timed to favour speech development while limiting disturbance of midface growth. The two aims pull in opposite directions, which is why timing is a team decision rather than a calendar date.

Later stages include alveolar bone grafting for the alveolar gap and, for maxillary undergrowth, orthognathic surgery near growth completion. Each stage is planned at the cleft clinic, never as an isolated booking.

teach.heading: Ears, speech and teeth run alongside
teach.body:
Audiological surveillance through childhood catches the middle ear fluid that follows palate clefts, with ventilation tubes where hearing suffers. A child who cannot hear cannot build speech, whatever the palate looks like.

Speech and language therapy runs through childhood, with secondary surgery such as pharyngoplasty where velopharyngeal leak persists. Orthodontic care aligns the displaced segments and teeth around the grafted alveolus.

teach.heading: The team, the family and the system
teach.body:
Care is delivered by a multidisciplinary cleft team spanning surgery, orthodontics, speech therapy, audiology, ENT, genetics and psychology, with family counselling where a syndrome is found. No single clinic can substitute for it.

In India, refer early to a cleft centre: district early-intervention and RBSK pathways cover repair for eligible children, and Ayushman Bharat empanelled centres admit listed procedures cashlessly. Name the next appointment and the feeding helpline before the family leaves.

probes.q: What feeding measures start at diagnosis, before any operation?
probes.a: Upright positioning, expressed milk by cup and spoon or soft bottle, small frequent feeds, special teats or plates, and weekly weight review.

probes.q: Why is palate closure timed rather than done as early as possible?
probes.a: Earlier closure favours speech but disturbs midface growth, so timing balances intelligible speech against maxillary undergrowth as a team decision.

probes.q: A five year old with a repaired palate still has nasal speech and normal hearing. What next?
probes.a: Speech reassessment with nasendoscopy for velopharyngeal closure, continued therapy, and consideration of secondary surgery such as pharyngoplasty.

sources.source: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.treatment.cleft.management.dosingNote: This module teaches management at the level of principles and referral: feeding method, staged surgery, hearing and speech surveillance, and team care. Drug choices and anaesthetic detail follow the treating cleft team's protocol at the time of care. CliniX does not prescribe.

cases.title: A mother whose baby feeds for an hour and is not gaining
cases.opening: Sunita Pawar, 24, carries in her 4-month-old daughter Aarohi, who has had a gap in her upper lip since birth. The baby is alert but small. Sunita says feeds take nearly an hour and milk comes out of the nose. Introduce yourself and take a history from the mother.
cases.fallback: I am not sure what you mean, doctor. Can you ask that a different way?

patient.name: Aarohi Pawar
patient.residence: Rural, lives with parents and grandmother in a village near Solapur

cues: what brings you today
what is the problem with the baby
why have you come to the hospital
tell me about your baby
how can i help your child
presenting.reply: Doctor, my daughter was born with this gap in her lip. She feeds for nearly an hour and milk comes out of her nose, and she is not gaining weight like my neighbour's baby.

cues: when was the gap first noticed
was the gap seen at birth
how long has the cleft been there
did you notice it just after delivery
birth_noticed.reply: It was there from birth itself. The nurse who conducted the delivery said it is a cleft lip and sent us here, but we could come only now.

cues: which side is the gap on
is the gap on one side or both
does the gap reach the nose
how far up does the cleft go
lip_gap_side.reply: It is on the left side only. The gap runs from her lip right up into her nose, and her left nostril looks flat.

cues: is there a hole in the roof of the mouth
does the palate also have a gap
have you looked inside her mouth
is the cleft only in the lip
palate_gap.reply: Yes, there is a big opening in the roof of her mouth too. When she cries I can see right up inside. Nobody told us the inside is also open.

cues: does milk come out of the nose
nasal regurgitation during feeds
milk escaping through the nostrils
leakage of feeds from the nose
milk_nasal_leak.reply: Yes, every feed some milk bubbles out of her nose, especially when she cries and feeds at the same time. It frightens my mother-in-law.

cues: how long does one feed take
how often do you feed her
is the baby able to suck well
does she tire during breastfeeding
feed_duration.reply: Nearly three quarters of an hour each time, and I feed her eight to ten times a day and night. She sucks weakly, stops often, and falls asleep tired without finishing.

cues: what was her birth weight
how much does she weigh now
is she gaining weight properly
what does the growth card show
weight_trend.reply: She was born at two and three quarter kilos. Now at four months she is only five kilos, and the anganwadi card shows her line going flat. The nurse said she should be heavier.

cues: is her breathing noisy
any difficulty in breathing
does she stop breathing in sleep
snoring sounds or blue spells
noisy_breathing.reply: No, her breathing is quiet. She sleeps on her back peacefully and I have never seen her turn blue or stop breathing.

cues: any discharge from the ears
repeated ear infections
pus coming from the ear
has she had ear discharge
ear_discharge.reply: No discharge so far. Her ears look normal from outside and she has never had fever with ear pain.

cues: does she turn to sounds
response to your voice
does she startle to loud sounds
hearing response when called
sound_response.reply: Yes, she turns when I call her name and startles when the steel plate falls. She seems to hear normally.

cues: what sounds does she make
cooing and babbling milestones
does she make gurgling sounds
vocal sounds for her age
cooing_babble.reply: She coos and gurgles like other babies, aaa and ooo sounds. She has not started babbling yet but the health worker said that comes later.

cues: did you attend antenatal checkups
how many pregnancy visits did you have
was this a hospital pregnancy
antenatal care during this pregnancy
pregnancy_care.reply: I went to the primary health centre three times. The pregnancy was normal, no swelling of feet and no fits. Delivery was normal at the rural hospital.

cues: did you take folic acid tablets
iron tablets in pregnancy
when did you start the pregnancy tablets
regular antenatal tablets
folic_iron.reply: I got iron tablets but started them only in the fifth month, and I missed many days because they made me nauseous. Nobody gave me folic acid separately that I remember.

cues: tobacco or alcohol during pregnancy
did you chew tobacco while pregnant
smoke exposure at home
country liquor in pregnancy
tobacco_liquor_home.reply: I never chewed tobacco or drank liquor. But my husband smokes bidis inside the house, so the smoke was always around me.

cues: anyone in the family with a similar gap
clefts running in the family
lip pits in parents or relatives
previous child with a birth defect
family_lip_pits.reply: Nobody in our family has this. My first son is normal. My husband and I have no pits or marks on our lips.

cues: where was the baby delivered
who conducted the delivery
was any doctor present at birth
place of delivery and birth care
delivery_place.reply: At the rural hospital nearby, conducted by the nurse sister. A doctor saw the baby the next morning, wrote a slip for the cleft clinic at the district hospital, and told us to feed with a spoon.

skill.gen.appearance.finding: Alert 4-month-old girl, small for age, active and pink. Left upper lip shows a wide gap running into the nostril. No dysmorphic features beyond the cleft, no limb anomalies.

skill.gen.vitals.finding: Heart rate 138 per minute, respiratory rate 36 per minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature normal. Weight 5.0 kg, below the expected curve with a flattening growth line.

skill.exam.surg.buccal_mucosa.finding: Complete cleft of the left upper lip running the full height into the nostril floor. Left ala flattened with the columella pulled to the left. Right lip and both commissures normal.

skill.exam.surg.maxilla.finding: Notched alveolus on the left with a visible gap in the gum ridge. Premaxilla in midline, not displaced forward. No bilateral involvement.

skill.exam.surg.floor_of_mouth.finding: Wide cleft of the soft palate continuing through the hard palate to the alveolar notch. Nasal septum attached to the right palatal shelf. Uvula halves separated, tonsils normal.

skill.exam.surg.cervical_nodes.finding: No palpable submental, submandibular or jugular nodes on either side. Neck supple, no midline or lateral swelling.

hearing_assess.label: Hearing assessment with tympanometry
hearing_assess.note: Every palate cleft needs a hearing baseline and repeated checks, because fluid comes and goes while speech is being built.
hearing_assess.result: Response to voice present clinically. Formal audiology booked at the district hospital: middle ear function to be charted before palate repair.

growth_review.label: Growth chart review and feeding plan
growth_review.note: The flat weight line is the objective proof that feeding support cannot wait for any operation.
growth_review.result: Weight 5.0 kg at four months against a birth weight near 2.75 kg: faltering growth. Cup and spoon feeds with expressed milk, upright positioning, weekly weighing advised.

cleft_team.label: Referral to the cleft team
cleft_team.note: Repair is staged by a team, never booked as a single operation from this clinic.
cleft_team.result: Referred to the district cleft clinic for surgical, orthodontic, speech and ENT review with RBSK paperwork started.

karyotype.label: Karyotype and microarray
karyotype.note: Not indicated as a first step here: examination shows an isolated cleft with no extra anomaly, normal growth apart from feeding, and no family pattern. It is reconsidered only if a syndrome feature appears.

echo.label: Echocardiography
echo.note: Not indicated routinely: no murmur, no sweating or breathlessness on feeds, and no syndrome feature. A murmur or desaturation would change this at once.

speech_review.label: Speech and language review
speech_review.note: Formal assessment waits until babbling age and after palate closure, but the referral is made now so the child is in the system.
speech_review.result: Referred to speech therapy for babble monitoring and later velopharyngeal assessment.

differentialModel.answer: Complete unilateral left cleft lip and palate. Consider Pierre Robin sequence, Van der Woude syndrome, an atypical facial cleft, and a submucous component with middle ear effusion.

diagnosis.answer: Complete unilateral left cleft lip and palate, Veau group three, with feeding difficulty and faltering growth, isolated on current assessment.

managementModel.answer: Urgent feeding support with cup and spoon and weekly growth review, hearing surveillance, referral to the multidisciplinary cleft team for staged lip and palate repair with speech therapy and orthodontic follow-up.

teachingPoints: The palate, not the lip, decides feeding: the gap breaks suction, so milk escapes through the nose, feeds run long, and the growth card flattens.
Completeness is read at the nostril: this gap runs the full height into the nostril floor with a flattened ala, which is what complete means.
Quiet breathing, a midline premaxilla and no extra anomaly keep this isolated: noisy breathing with a small jaw would have meant Pierre Robin and an airway-first plan.
No lip pits and no affected relative keep Van der Woude out today, but the lips of both parents are still part of the examination.
Hearing is assessed by machine, not by impression: a baby who startles can still carry middle ear fluid that will cost speech later.
